flawed_step: The first step fails: going from "every edge lies in exactly one triangle" to "some vertex is adjacent to every other vertex." Nothing in the hypothesis forces a shared vertex. The friendship theorem assumes that every pair of vertices has exactly one common neighbour, which is a much stronger condition. The edge-triangle condition is local, and the graph does not even have to be connected.
counterexample: Take G to be two disjoint triangles, with vertices {1,2,3} and {4,5,6} and edges 12, 13, 23, 45, 46, 56. Each edge is in exactly one triangle: 12 is only in 123, and the same holds for the others. Every vertex has degree 2, but a universal vertex would need degree 5, so there isn't one. A connected counterexample also exists: the 3x3 rook's graph K3□K3. Its vertices are (i,j) with i,j in {1,2,3}, and two vertices are adjacent when they share a row or a column. An edge within a row has exactly one common neighbour, the third vertex of that row. A vertex in a different row and column is adjacent to at most one endpoint of the edge. So each edge is in exactly one triangle. The graph has 9 vertices and every vertex has degree 4 < 8, so there is no universal vertex.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The edge-triangle condition does not force a universal vertex. Two disjoint triangles are a counterexample, and so is the connected graph K3□K3 (9 vertices, each of degree 4). In both, every edge lies in exactly one triangle, but no vertex is adjacent to all the others.
